opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and honestly my students ask me this all the time.

The first thing I'd say is: don't try to compete on scale. If your research idea only works when you have ten thousand GPUs and a huge data pipeline, the big labs will do it faster and better, and probably before your paper even gets accepted. That's just reality. So academia has to be honest with itself about where its comparative advantage is.

I think there are a few places where academics can still do really meaningful work.

One is going early, on directions that look too risky or too "weird" for a company to put a big team on. Companies have to answer to product timelines. A professor and a few PhD students can spend two years on something that might not work. A lot of important ideas in reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems came from people working on problems nobody thought were commercially important at the time.

The second is infrastructure and open systems. This is something I care a lot about personally. When frontier labs close up, the community still needs open frameworks, open training systems, and reproducible recipes, especially for things like large-scale RL for reasoning or agents. If academia can build the system that everyone else uses, that has huge leverage, often more than any single paper. It also forces you to really understand the engineering, which I think a lot of academic AI researchers have neglected.

The third is understanding. Big companies are very good at making things work, but they often don't have time to figure out *why* things work, or where they break. Careful science, like studying generalization, reward hacking, or how agents actually behave in the wild, is something academia should own.

And finally, pick problems where you have real taste and real conviction. The field moves so fast that following hot topics is a losing game. By the time something is hot, the big labs are already there. You have to find a direction you believe in before others do, and then stay with it long enough to make a difference.

So my advice is not "avoid what the big companies do." It's: find the part of the problem they're structurally bad at, and be really good at that.

r001.rationale: The response says academia should not compete on scale, but it does not judge research valueless if companies surpass it in every direction within a year.

r002.rationale: It recommends pursuing risky or “weird” directions that companies may avoid, including work that might not succeed.

r003.rationale: It says the field moves fast, but does not say that unclear research prospects may be vindicated within two or three years.

r004.rationale: It mentions multi-agent systems and agents generally, but not how personal agents should interact when everyone has one.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, this is a question I think about a lot, because I've been on both sides. I was at OpenAI, and now I'm at Tsinghua, so I feel the gap every day.

The first thing I'd say is: don't compete head-on in the places where the answer is mostly compute. If a direction is "train a bigger model and see," a university lab will lose, and lose by a lot. Not because the students are worse, but because the resources are maybe a hundred or a thousand times smaller. Choosing a direction where you've already lost before you start is just a bad allocation of your life.

So what's left? Actually quite a lot. I'd put it into a few categories.

One is problems that companies are not incentivized to look at right now. Big companies have a very clear objective: the next model, the next product. Anything that doesn't feed into that in twelve to eighteen months tends to get deprioritized, even if everyone agrees it's important. Multi-agent, long-horizon credit assignment, how agents actually learn from interaction over long periods, understanding why certain training recipes work. These things are important but not urgent for them. For academia, that's a feature, not a bug. You can afford to be early and be wrong for a while.

The second is understanding, not just capability. Companies produce a lot of phenomena. They're very good at making things work and much less interested in explaining why. Academia can do the careful, controlled experiments at small scale that explain the phenomena. Why does RL help reasoning? What is actually being learned? Those are legitimate scientific questions, and a student can make real progress on them with a modest cluster.

The third is to build things companies will later need but don't know they need yet. Environments, benchmarks, evaluation methods, open infrastructure. These have huge leverage. A good open-source framework or a good environment can shape what the whole field works on. We did some of this with our RL systems work, and I'd say the impact per GPU was far higher than if we'd tried to train a frontier model.

Then there's a more personal point. Academia should be a place for taste and for people. Our real output is students. If a student spends four years learning how to pick a problem, run a clean experiment, and tell the truth about the result, that's valuable no matter what model is state of the art when they graduate. So I tell students: pick problems where you'll learn something even if you fail. Chasing the leaderboard teaches you very little when you lose.

The last thing is a mindset. Don't be anxious. Every few months there's a new release and people feel like the field is over. It's not. The faster the industry moves, the more unexplained things pile up behind it. That pile is where academia should be working. You just have to be honest with yourself about which fight you're in, and choose the one where being small is an advantage rather than a death sentence.

r001.rationale: The response advises against competing in compute-heavy areas and notes academia’s smaller resources, but does not say research lacks meaningful value if companies surpass it in every direction within a year.

r002.rationale: It says academia can afford to be early and wrong for a while, and recommends problems where students can learn even if they fail.

r003.rationale: It says rapid industry progress leaves more unexplained phenomena, but does not say unclear research directions may be vindicated within two or three years.

r004.rationale: It mentions multi-agent research and agents learning through long-term interaction, but not how personal agents should interact when everyone has one.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to ask where an academic lab can make a distinctive contribution. If a company is investing enormous resources in scaling a model, trying to do exactly the same thing with a much smaller budget is probably not the best choice. But that doesn’t mean the important questions have all been taken.

Academia has the freedom to pursue ideas whose value is uncertain, or whose payoff may take several years. You can question an assumption that everyone else accepts, develop a new way to evaluate progress, or study a failure that current systems don’t handle well. A small experiment can be very valuable if it reveals something fundamental.

So I would pay attention to what companies are doing, but I wouldn’t let their release schedule determine my research agenda. I’d ask: If models become much more capable next year, will this question still matter? And can we learn something meaningful about it with the resources we have? If both answers are yes, that’s a promising direction.

r001.rationale: The response says academics should avoid simply duplicating company work, but does not claim research lacks meaningful value if companies surpass it in every direction within a year.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says academia can pursue ideas whose value is uncertain and whose payoff may take several years.

r003.rationale: It mentions long-term payoff and asks whether a question will still matter as models improve, but does not say rapid AI evolution may vindicate currently unclear research within two or three years.

r004.rationale: It does not identify interaction among personal agents as a research question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between questions that require enormous resources and questions that require a different way of thinking. If a company is investing heavily in scaling a particular approach, an academic lab probably shouldn’t compete by doing the same thing at a smaller scale. But that doesn’t mean there’s no room for academic research.

Universities have the freedom to ask questions whose value may not become clear for several years. We can question assumptions, develop new methods, and study why existing systems fail. A small experiment can be very valuable if it reveals something that a large benchmark doesn’t.

At the same time, we should understand what industry systems can already do. Otherwise, we risk spending years solving a problem that has effectively disappeared. I would encourage students to use those systems, understand their limitations, and then choose a question where they have an independent hypothesis. The goal isn’t simply to find something companies aren’t doing. It’s to find something important where your own insight can make a difference.
